conversation.content:
Hello—thank you so much for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Maya Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood.

We’re going to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a gentle way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days—things like mood, anxiety, sleep, appetite, and any scary thoughts. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll move through ten questions, one at a time, and I’ll ask them in everyday language so it feels more like a conversation than a test.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you still been able to look forward to things you normally enjoy, or has that feeling of enjoyment been missing most of the time?

[Soft sigh, eyes a little glassy]  
I still want to enjoy things… but it’s like the color’s been drained out. When I think about grabbing coffee with a friend or even just binge-watching a show, I tell myself I *should* feel excited, but mostly I just feel flat—like I’m going through the motions for a minute, then I’m tired again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]  
Sometimes a little giggle slips out—like when the baby makes those silly milk bubbles—but it feels forced, like I’m reminding myself “this is supposed to be funny.” Most of the time I just feel too worn-out to really laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow head shake, voice quiet]

Not really… I keep hoping I’ll feel that spark, but even planning a simple walk or ordering my favorite food feels like one more chore. Everything just lands on the “meh” side—like I’m watching life through frosted glass.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Glances down, twisting the edge of my robe tie]

Yeah… like when the baby wouldn’t settle last night, my brain jumped straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I know rationally he’s just fussy sometimes, but I still catch myself thinking, “If I were a better mom, he’d sleep.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Presses lips together, fingers drumming on knee]

Pretty often. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly my chest feels tight—no real reason. I worry the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, or that I’ll trip on the stairs with him. It’s like my brain’s always scanning for danger, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week—like yesterday in the grocery store—my heart started racing out of nowhere and I felt shaky, like I had to grip the cart so I wouldn’t drop him. Nothing bad was happening, but the panic just surged up. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me rattled the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, folding—three more pile up. Dishes in the sink, texts I haven’t answered, my own shower I keep postponing. I’m not drowning exactly, but it’s like I’m always half a step behind and my energy’s just gone.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Exhales slowly, rubbing my eyes]

A few nights this week I’d finally get him down, but then my mind just wouldn’t quit—running through everything I might have forgotten or imagined worst-case stuff. I lie there staring at the ceiling, drifting in and out, so I’m still tired when he wakes up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Shoulders sag a little]

Yeah... there’ve been moments—especially in the late afternoon—where this heavy sadness just settles in. Nothing specific happened, but I feel weepy and kind of hollow, like I miss something but don’t know what. It usually lifts after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really... my eyes sting sometimes, but the tears don’t come. I feel like I could cry, but it just sits in my throat. Only once this week—when he wouldn’t latch at 3 a.m.—did a couple tears slip out, and even then I wiped them away fast.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Shakes head quickly]

No—never. I could never leave my baby like that. I’m exhausted and low, but I want to be here for him.

You've shared how the joy and colour seem to have drained from everyday moments since your baby arrived, leaving you feeling flat, weepy and constantly on edge. Despite loving your little one fiercely, you find yourself weighed down by a heavy sadness, self-blame when things go wrong, and sudden waves of panic or worry that appear without warning, making it hard to rest even when the house is quiet.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter and feeling too worn-out to laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Response shows near-complete loss of pleasure and anticipation, clear depressive anhedonia</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports self-blame "some of the time" (when baby fussy), aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic with physical symptoms (racing heart, shakiness) occurring multiple times in the week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling persistently behind and depleted, indicating intermittent difficulty coping while still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated sleep disruption from racing thoughts and anxiety "a few nights this week," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring heavy sadness, weepiness, and a hollow feeling, indicating sadness "quite often" but not "most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 19 (≥14 indicates probable major depression); Q2, Q8, Q9 show persistent low mood and loss of pleasure meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>; Q4, Q5 reveal frequent anxiety and panic; Q7 documents insomnia secondary to racing thoughts; Q3 demonstrates inappropriate guilt; Q6 confirms feeling overwhelmed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent review with your <med>GP/obstetrician</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health team</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med> or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Ask about practical support: home help, partner/family sharing night duties, and local <med>postpartum support groups</med]
4. Begin gentle daily routine: short outdoor walks, balanced meals, hydration, and brief rest when baby sleeps
5. Keep emergency numbers handy (your maternity unit, <med>national crisis lines</med>) and return for re-screening in two weeks or sooner if thoughts of self-harm develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, 2 wks post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, panic attacks without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to rumination (Q7)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to cope (Q6)  
- Subjective loss of energy (Q1, Q6)

Pattern  
High affective distress (depression + anxiety clusters) with intact reality testing; no self-harm ideation reported (Q10).

Screening significance  
Score suggests probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety in postpartum context; no current safety concerns.

Next step  
Recommend formal clinical assessment (PHQ-9/GAD-7, clinician interview) and discussion of support / treatment options.
